title: Plastic Alternatives
desc: Understand materials that can replace single-use plastic, how to test them honestly, and how to plan a small product switch.
outcomes: Explain plastic types and the problem of waste.
Test an alternative for use and cost.
Judge claims such as biodegradable and compostable.
Plan a product switch for a small business.
task: Choose one single-use plastic item, test two alternatives, compare cost and impact, and write a switch plan with customer message.
condition: Samples of items, a scale and basic tools, a spreadsheet, two peers and a mentor. Safe, non-food-contact tests unless approved.
standard: Tests are repeatable; claims are checked against recognised definitions; cost per use is shown; end-of-life route exists locally; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Shop owners, packaging buyers, students, municipal staff.
evidence: test sheet, comparison table, switch plan
modules: The plastic waste problem
Understand
Single-use plastic is used for minutes and can last for centuries. Understanding the scale helps you choose where to act first.
Single-use items such as bags, bottles, sachets and cutlery make up a large share of litter.
Microplastics from breakdown and from textiles enter water and food.
Order of action: reduce, reuse, recycle, and only then replace.
A switch that increases total impact is not an improvement.
A cafe counts 300 disposable cups a day. Switching to a returnable cup scheme with a deposit cuts that by 70 per cent, more than any new compostable cup could.
Audit the plastic you or your business use in one week and list items with counts.
List has at least 15 items with counts and the top three are highlighted.
Plastic types and codes
Understand
Knowing the type tells you if it can be recycled.
Resin codes 1 to 7 show the polymer type.
PET (1) and HDPE (2) are widely recycled; films and multilayer packs are rarely recycled.
Mixed, dirty and black plastics are hard to sort.
Check local collection rules.
PET bottles are often collected and recycled; a chips packet made of multilayer film usually goes to landfill.
Sort 10 items by code and recyclability in your area.
At least 9 sorted correctly.
Alternative materials
Understand
Many options exist, each with trade-offs.
Paper, card, glass, metal, plant fibres, starch-based plastics and compostable blends.
Reuse systems often beat single-use alternatives.
Consider strength, moisture, heat and cost.
Consider whether local facilities exist for the end-of-life route.
A bakery tests paper bags, starch bags and reusable cloth bags. The paper bag works but costs more; a cloth bag discount scheme reduces bag use by half.
Make an options table for one product with pros and cons.
At least four options compared.
Testing alternatives
Apply
Do real tests before switching.
Strength: load until failure; leak test; heat test; shelf life.
Repeat each test three times.
Record failures and costs.
Test with real users.
A starch bag tears at 3 kg while a paper bag holds 5 kg; the shop selects paper for heavy items.
Test two alternatives against your current item and record results.
Table has repeated results and a conclusion.
Life-cycle thinking
Analyse
Look at the whole life of a product, from raw material to disposal.
Stages: raw material, making, transport, use, end of life.
A reusable item wins after enough uses.
Local conditions change results.
State your boundaries.
A glass jar needs about 12 uses to beat a plastic tub in emissions; a thicker cup needs 20 uses.
Do a simple comparison for two options.
Method and sources stated.
Claims and labels
Evaluate
Avoid being misled by green claims.
Biodegradable and compostable are not the same.
Compostable may need industrial facilities.
Look for recognised standards and test reports.
Ask for evidence.
A bag labelled "eco" has no standard. The buyer asks for a test report and finds it is not compostable in home conditions.
Review three labels and score their claims.
Each review lists evidence required.
Customers and cost
Evaluate
A switch must work for customers and the business.
Cost per use, not per piece.
Deposit or discount schemes.
Explain simply and train staff.
Track complaints.
A refill discount repays the cost of the container within 20 uses.
Cost your switch for one month.
Currency shown.
Switch plan
Create
Plan and review.
Steps, dates, owners, measures.
Pilot in one store.
Report results.
Scale or adjust.
Plastic bags fall by 70 per cent in one month with a returnable bag scheme.
Present the plan.
Measures are clear.
quiz: Order of waste actions?
Reduce, reuse, recycle. (Covered in module 1: The plastic waste problem. To pass that module: List has at least 15 items with counts and the top three are highlighted.)
Why microplastics matter?
They enter food and water. (Covered in module 2: Plastic types and codes. To pass that module: At least 9 sorted correctly.)
Compostable equals biodegradable?
No. (Covered in module 3: Alternative materials. To pass that module: At least four options compared.)
Name a test.
Strength, leak, heat or shelf life. (Covered in module 4: Testing alternatives. To pass that module: Table has repeated results and a conclusion.)
Life-cycle stages?
Material, making, transport, use, end of life. (Covered in module 5: Life-cycle thinking. To pass that module: Method and sources stated.)
Why cost per use?
Reuse items spread cost. (Covered in module 6: Claims and labels. To pass that module: Each review lists evidence required.)
Name a label risk.
Greenwashing. (Covered in module 7: Customers and cost. To pass that module: Currency shown.)
Best first step?
Reduce. (Covered in module 8: Switch plan. To pass that module: Measures are clear.)
Why pilot?
Test small first. (Covered in module 8: Switch plan. To pass that module: Measures are clear.)
Why local end-of-life?
Facilities differ. (Covered in module 8: Switch plan. To pass that module: Measures are clear.)
rubric: Every claim linked to a dated record and checked by a peer
Checked, dated and explained to others
